extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, actors, and cultivated readers of drama (English stage writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and critical criteria for composing and performing English tragedy (verse, plot, diction, and stage-behaviour), plus related norms about affectation and choice of reading material for personal improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation / act naturally
rubrics_metrics.description: Affectation is the self-consciousness that 'employs the Consciousness in too fondly approving a Man's own Conceptions' and turns beauty or wit into deformity or absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs and examples: fixed attention to some personal charm expressed in every look, word, and gesture (e.g. widening the lips to show teeth, pointing a fan to display an arm, adjusting a tucker to recover a pose). Remedy: fix the heart upon the chief design of life; be indifferent to small perfections; 'contemn little Merits'; allow praise to be shown by others' actions rather than seeking immediate compliments. The best way to throw off a fondness for praise is to abstain from seeking it in indifferent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize signs of affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Affectation betrays itself by interruptions of natural gesture and by behaviour aimed at obtaining notice or applause rather than expressing sincere feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: continual change of airs and attitudes to 'strike the Hearts of their Beholders'; overattention to dress or a single well-chosen article (cravat, hat, coat); a person 'looking about for Applause' or 'laying Traps' to be commended. These are anti-patterns to avoid in social performance and writing about characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep public speech and behaviour to purpose (avoid performative cleverness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affectation creeps into public places (the Bar, the Pulpit) as impertinencies, premeditated speeches that run from the purpose, quaint phrases, or witty declamation used for effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the bar and in the pulpit, speakers should avoid superfluities, unnecessary 'quaint Phrases', impertinent wit, and theatrical humility expressed in overly well-turned phrases. The counsel: be close and logical at the Bar; in the Pulpit avoid inflaming passion into mere raillery or ornamental display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer English blank verse (iambic) for tragedy; avoid rhyme and mixing metres
rubrics_metrics.description: Blank verse is the most proper metre for English tragedy because it lifts discourse above prose while remaining near ordinary speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid plays in rhyme (as absurd in English as hexameters in Greek/Latin), and avoid mixing scenes in rhyme with scenes in blank verse ('two several Languages'). Allowance: a poet may conclude a tragedy or an act with two or three couplets (like an Italian Opera air) or use a variety of numbers to relieve the ear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary verse numbers and use hemistichs or abrupt pauses to express passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity of numbers prevents the ear from being tired and abrupt pauses can suit expressed passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devices permitted: concluding speeches with a hemistick (half verse), abrupt breakings-off in the middle of a verse, and other irregularities when they 'humour any Passion that is expressed by it.' These are acceptable to enhance dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize noble thought (sentiment) over sonorous but empty expression
rubrics_metrics.description: A noble sentiment in plain language is preferable to a vulgar sentiment dressed in pompous expression; sense should carry expression, not be overwhelmed by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice: before versifying, lay down the whole contexture of dialogue in plain English; judge the 'naked Thought' of each speech when divested of tragic ornaments. This prevents being 'imposed upon by Words' and helps ensure thoughts are natural and worthy of the speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pompous phrases and forced metaphors where passions and manners are represented
rubrics_metrics.description: Sounding phrases, hard metaphors, and forced expressions often obscure or depress great thoughts and are especially injurious in parts where opinions, manners, and passions are represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's rule (quoted): expression should be laboured in unactive parts (descriptions, similitudes, narrations), but not where passions are shown. Example criticism: Shakespeare often faults here—grand language obscuring true sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour expression in descriptive/unactive parts, not in passionate representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Elaborate and laboured expressions are more appropriate to unactive portions of the fable (descriptions, similitudes, narrations) than to passages representing passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rich diction for narrative/descriptive passages, but keep representation of opinions, manners, and passions clear and less pompous to avoid obscuring meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use natural diction in passionate parts; avoid undue familiarity in dignified contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Following nature in the language of tragedy succeeds in passionate parts, but excessive familiarity of phrase in dignified passages is a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Otway excels by following natural speech in passion; however, he sometimes uses phrases too familiar for parts that by Aristotle's rule ought to be raised by dignity of expression. Adjust register to suit the scene and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy need not enforce poetical justice; unhappy endings can be superior
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that tragedies must distribute rewards and punishments equally (poetical justice) has no foundation in nature or ancient practice; tragedies that end unhappily often produce stronger terror and commiseration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle noted that tragedies ending unhappily pleased audiences and won prizes; making virtue always triumphant weakens the tragic effect because audiences anticipate recovery. Permit virtuous characters to suffer or perish when the fable demands it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tragi-comedy and ill-related double plots (or make the under-plot closely related)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragi-comedy (mixing mirth and sorrow) is a 'monstrous' invention that dilutes tragic effect; double plots divert grief from the principal action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an under-plot is used, ensure it bears a near relation to the principal design and is concluded by the same catastrophe so as to contribute to, rather than dilute, the main tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'rants' and bombast in tragic writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Rants—vehemence, bombast, unnatural exclamations, curses, vows, blasphemies—are false beauties that often please audiences but are not true greatness of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: poets and actors adding vehemence where there is no passion, inflating lines to create applause (actors like Powell raising applause by rant). Result: 'Bombast' replaces true sentiment. Strive for just, natural passion rather than swelling, fustian language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't contrive characters' behaviour merely to please a segment of the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Crafting a hero who behaves insolently towards men but abjectly before a mistress to charm the ladies is an artificial method that panders to bad taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: such inconsistent or designed shifts in behaviour (insolence to some, abjection to others) are 'false Beauties' and should not be adopted as a recipe for genuine dramatic admiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose reading material that enlightens the understanding and rectifies the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: For personal improvement (especially of women in the author's example), prefer books that 'enlighten the Understanding and rectify the Passions' rather than those that merely divert the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author promises to recommend specific books suitable for the improvement of the sex in another paper; the principle is to favour instructive, morally corrective works over romances whose chief use is diversion.
